title: The bungas
hook: the misls built rest-houses round the sacred pool for pilgrims and defenders

segments.voice: Yesterday, twice a year at Amritsar: the whole Khalsa gathered at Vaisakhi and Diwali to agree a gurmata before the Guru Granth Sahib. Your line was decide before the guru. Which decision did you slow down? Today, where all those riders slept. Day nine hundred one.

A blanket unrolled on a brick floor, a few steps from the water. A horse tied up outside. A rider who has come a long way leaves his things in a room with thick walls and goes down to bathe in the pool and bow at the Harmandir. That room isn't an inn. Sikh histories say the misls built such houses. Around the sacred pool, one by one, they rose, each put up by a chief or a band. Today's word is what those houses were called: bunga.
screen: `A BLANKET ON A BRICK FLOOR.` → `A FEW STEPS FROM THE WATER.` → `HOUSES RISE AROUND THE POOL.`

segments.voice: A bunga did three jobs at once. The first was rest. Pilgrims coming to the Harmandir needed somewhere to stay, and a bunga gave them a place by the pool: close enough to hear the kirtan, the sung scripture. The guest didn't have to find an inn or bargain for a room. The house was already there, built for exactly this. The second job was defense. These were years when the Harmandir had been attacked and damaged, as this path has told. So a bunga was not a light little guesthouse. Tradition describes them as strong buildings, some with high walls, where defenders could stay and keep watch over the pool and the shrine. Rest and guard duty under the same roof. The third job was a quiet one: belonging. Each bunga was tied to a misl, a chief, or a community, so when riders from that band arrived, they knew where their place was. Their bunga. A misl that might be miles away the rest of the year had a doorway on the edge of the sacred pool. And one building connected to this story is worth naming. Some histories call the building of the Akal Takht itself the Akal Bunga. Whatever the label, it sits facing the Harmandir across the causeway. Over the years the precinct around the pool has been rebuilt, and most of the old bungas have gone, though a few still stand. But the idea is worth keeping: around the Harmandir, the people built rooms for strangers to rest in. Rest by the pool.
screen: `A PLACE TO REST BY THE POOL.` · `STRONG WALLS FOR THE DEFENDERS.` · `A DOORWAY FOR EVERY BAND.` · `THE AKAL BUNGA.` · then, large: `REST BY THE POOL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes about rest you can offer. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Now bring to mind someone who is tired right now: a friend with a new baby, a parent working two jobs, a colleague who's carrying too much, someone far from home. Ask yourself what a bunga would look like for them. A couch for the night. An hour of quiet while you take the kids. A meal they don't have to cook. A message that says, come over, you don't have to talk. Choose one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bunga. A rest-house built by a misl or chief beside the sacred pool at Amritsar, for pilgrims to stay and for defenders to keep watch. Today's word.
Your line: rest by the pool. Today, offer one tired person a place to rest: a seat, a meal, an evening, an hour. Day nine hundred one.

howItsDone: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib today stay in the guest houses (sarais) of the complex, free of charge, and some old bunga buildings still stand near the pool.

notes: Bungas built by misls, chiefs and communities, with defenders lodged in them: framed as 'Sikh histories say' / 'tradition describes'. Confirm.
'Some histories call the building of the Akal Takht itself the Akal Bunga': confirm.
'The precinct has been rebuilt, and the old bungas with it': no count of survivors given; confirm. The Ramgarhia Bunga (tomorrow's lesson) is the best-known survivor and is not named here.
howItsDone: free stay in the complex's sarais; confirm wording.
Editor: rewrote the hook, a third arrival-at-Amritsar opening in a row (days 887 and 900), to open on an object; cut 'through the night' from the kirtan line as unsupported.
